newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president inherits crisis, unrest.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president inherits crisis, unrest.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov formally took office in a colourful religious and military ceremony on Wednesday, inheriting economic crisis, political deadlock and nationwide unrest.

Stoyanov took over command of the army from outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev at a military parade outside the presidency, then received the blessing of the Orthodox church in the first religious ceremony for a new head of state since Boris III became king in October 1918.

A 21-gun salute rang out as the red, white and green national flag was raised near the Alexander Nevsky cathedral, scene of daily opposition protests for general elections and against a new cabinet of the ex-communist ruling Socialists.
"I swear to give all my powers for the prosperity and strength of Bulgaria," Stoyanov said, swearing on an ornate bible at the open-air ceremony outside the mediaeval St Sofia church.
Bulgaria's Orthodox church has not been spared the divisions dogging the rest of society, but Stoyanov's religious ceremony included the two rival patriarchs.
Stoyanov received the blessing of Patriarch Pimen, who split from the synod with his followers after 1989, accusing the official Patriarch Maxim of being a stooge of the former communist regime.
Maxim, who said a separate mass for the new president in the gold-domed cathedral, greeted the president when he arrived for the blessing ceremony.
The president, who has cancelled the usual champagne reception as inappropriate at a time when hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians are hungry, laid a wreath at the memorial to the nation's war dead.
He then walked back to the presidency, surrounded by enthusiastic crowds who cheered him and booed outgoing Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov.
On Thursday Stoyanov, a lawyer who specialises in divorce cases, is to hold more talks with government and opposition on finding a way out of Bulgaria's political deadlock.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in presidential polls last November, backed calls for early elections at his swearing-in ceremony in parliament on Sunday.
"The new president looks more impressive than the previous one and I hope that his actions will be as statesmanlike as he looks," said engineer Petar Ivanov, one of the crowd at the presidency.

Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic whose president is a mainly ceremonial figure. He represents the country in its foreign relations, appoints ambassadors, judges and some other officials, and can veto laws once and send them back to parliament.
The president also has the task of asking the prime minister nominated by the largest parliamentary group to form a government, which Zhelev has refused to do in the present explosive atmosphere.
If the three main parliamentary groups fail to form a cabinet, the president must appoint a caretaker government, dissolve parliament and schedule elections within two months.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but want to form a second cabinet following Videnov's resignation last December 21. The opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) wants elections in March.
Videnov urged Stoyanov on Tuesday to hand the mandate to the Socialists' nominee for premier, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, saying he had a crisis programme ready.
The opposition blames Videnov for leading the country to the verge of default on its $10 billion foreign debt.

Government corruption and the Socialists' resistance to reform have left Bulgaria lagging behind other eastern European states. Annual inflation is running at more than 300 percent and a flight into dollars pushed the lev to a new all-time low on Wednesday of 800 to the dollar from about 70 a year ago.
